title: Fix It Before You Bin It. The Repair Guide That Starts With One Mistake
body: The mistake almost everyone makes with a broken household object happens in the first ten seconds, and it is not a tool mistake. It is a question mistake. The object stops working, and the question that jumps up is. What is broken? Wrong question. The right one is. What changed? Nothing fails without a cause, and most household failures have a cause that is visible, recent, and cheap to fix. So before anything else. Walk backwards through time. Did the problem start after a move, a drop, a cleaning, a battery change, a weather shift, a child with curious hands? Write down when you first noticed. The gap between the change and the symptom is where the repair lives, and finding it costs nothing. With that done, the patient path looks the same for almost every small object. Lamp, kettle, chair, fan, zipper, tap. Step one is the power and the fittings. Check what plugs in, screws in, snaps in. A surprising share of dead devices are just tired contacts, and reseating a plug, tightening a hinge screw, or cleaning a contact with a dry cloth returns more objects to life than any other single act in this guide. Count to thirty while you do it. Rushing here is how small repairs become big ones. Step two is looking before opening. Shine a light into the vents, the joints, the tracks. Cracked plastic, a pinched cable, a stripped thread, a build-up of lint. The eye finds these before the screwdriver does. If the problem needs an opening, take photos at every stage of disassembly. Your future self, holding three screws and zero memory, will send thanks. Step three is the honest diagnosis. Parts fail in patterns, and the pattern is almost always mechanical wear at a moving joint or a thermal failure at a heat source. Wiggling gently while the object runs, where safe, locates the loose joint. The hottest part of any failed device is always the prime suspect. Step four is the part worth the whole essay. Get the correct replacement, not the approximate one. The approximate screw strips. The approximate belt slips. The ten minutes saved on ordering the right part becomes an hour of fighting and a broken housing, and that is how a fixable object lands in the bin. Wait for the right part. The wait is part of the repair. Step five, reassembly, runs the photos backwards, every connector reseated, every screw started by hand before any tool touches it. Then the test, and then, this matters, the one-minute post-mortem. What was the cause, and what would prevent it repeating? A chair that broke from overloading gets a load rule. A socket that scorched gets a load check. The object taught a lesson; write it where you will meet it again. Notice what this process costs. Mostly minutes, a few units of money for parts, and attention paid slowly. Notice what it returns. An object that keeps working, a small set of proofs that your hands and eyes can be trusted, and one less thing in the stream of stuff heading to the bin. The repair habit grows from here on its own. The second fix is faster than the first, the tenth faster still, and somewhere along the way the reflex changes. A broken thing stops being a purchase and starts being a question. So, the question I hand over with the screwdriver. What is currently broken at your place, and what changed just before it broke?
